title: Help my unbelief (Mark 9:14–29)
hook: a father cries I do believe, Lord: help my unbelief

segments.voice: Yesterday, the mountain again: Jesus shining, a voice saying hear him, and then the walk back down. Your line was down the mountain. Who was at the bottom of yours? Today we meet who was at the bottom of theirs. Day two hundred sixteen.

If you've ever sat in a hospital hallway with someone you love behind the door, you know this father. Jesus comes down the mountain and walks into an argument. A crowd, some scribes, and the other disciples, who've failed. A man brought his son to them. Since childhood the boy has had fits: a spirit throws him down, he foams at the mouth, grinds his teeth, goes rigid. It has thrown him into fire and into water. The disciples tried and couldn't help. Now the father turns to Jesus, and he's too tired to be polite.
screen: `A HOSPITAL HALLWAY.` → `THE DISCIPLES COULDN'T HELP.` → `A FATHER TOO TIRED TO BE POLITE.`

segments.voice: First, the father's request. He says: if you can do anything, have compassion on us and help us. If you can. You can hear years of doctors and disappointments in those three words. Second, Jesus throws it back. In the Douay-Rheims: "If thou canst believe, all things are possible to him that believeth." The question isn't whether Jesus can. It's whether the father can believe. Third, the cry. Mark says the father cried out at once, with tears: "I do believe, Lord: help my unbelief." Both halves are true at the same time. I believe. I don't believe enough. Here's what's surprising: Jesus accepts it. He doesn't wait for a better, purer faith. He heals the boy with the faith this man actually has, half of it doubt. The boy goes still as a corpse, and people say he's dead. Jesus takes him by the hand and lifts him, and he stands up. Fourth, afterward, indoors. The disciples ask why they couldn't do it. He says, in the Douay: "This kind can go out by nothing, but by prayer and fasting." Many of the oldest Greek manuscripts have only prayer; the Latin Vulgate, which the Douay translates, has both. Either way the point is the same. The failure wasn't technique. It was that this needed prayer. Catholics have kept the father's cry for two thousand years. It's short enough to say in a hallway, and honest enough for the nights when faith is thin. Many saints who struggled with darkness prayed something very like it.
screen: `IF YOU CAN DO ANYTHING.` · `ALL THINGS ARE POSSIBLE TO HIM THAT BELIEVETH.` · `HE HEALS WITH THE FAITH THERE IS.` · `THIS KIND NEEDS PRAYER.` · then, large: `I DO BELIEVE, LORD: HELP MY UNBELIEF.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray the father's prayer, or sit with it. Settle and breathe. Notice how much you believe today, about God, about yourself, about anything that matters to you. Don't inflate it. Don't shrink it. Then, if you pray, say the father's words slowly on your breath: I do believe, Lord. Help my unbelief. Breathe in on the first half, out on the second. If you don't pray, simply let both be true at once, the part of you that trusts and the part that doesn't. The bell holds the time.
Help my unbelief. A father's cry, with tears, holding faith and doubt in one breath. And Jesus answers it. Today's word.
Your line: help my unbelief. Today, when doubt shows up, don't hide it or argue with it. Bring it along, the way the father did. Day two hundred sixteen.

screen: `DAY 216 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: A CHILD IN THE MIDDLE.`

howItsDone: Many Catholics use the father's words from Mark 9 as a short prayer in times of doubt, and the Church teaches that faith and questions can live together in a believer's life.

fork.setup: you're the father. Jesus says all things are possible to the one who believes. you believe, and you also don't. what do you say?
options: say you're not sure and walk away.
cry out that you believe, and ask for help with your unbelief.
fork.reveal: "I do believe, Lord: help my unbelief." he brings both halves, and Jesus heals his son.

original.note: Greek: help my unbelief. apistia is faith with a 'not' in front of it.

trapdoor: what you thought: a man who didn't have enough faith.
what it means: a father who holds belief and unbelief together, and brings both. Jesus answers with what's there.
what a scholar hears: pisteuō, boēthei mou tē apistia; and the 'and fasting' of 9:29 missing from many early Greek manuscripts.

notes: Douay-Rheims Mark 9:22, 9:23 and 9:28 given from memory; confirm wording and the one-verse offset from KJV numbering.
Textual note: 'and fasting' (kai nēsteia) is absent from Codex Sinaiticus and Vaticanus and present in many later manuscripts and the Vulgate; confirm phrasing 'many of the oldest Greek manuscripts'.
'Many saints who struggled with darkness prayed something very like it' is general and unattributed; a Keeper may want a specific example or to cut it.
The epilepsy-like symptoms are described as Mark describes them; the script does not diagnose. Confirm sensitivity.
